Content:
The graph of any cubic function [MATH: y = f(x)= ax^3 + bx^2 + cx +d] (where [MATH: a >0]) has a characteristic inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shape, with [MATH: y]-values ranging from [MATH: -\infty] to [MATH: +\infty.] This means that every such function has at least one real root and at most three distinct roots.

Content:
For instance, suppose that we want to plot the graph of [MATH: y = x^3-x.] Then we set [MATH: y=0] to find the roots:
[MATH: x^{3} − x|= 0; x(x^{2} − 1)|= 0; x(x − 1)(x + 1)|= 0]

Content:
By the zero-product rule, we get three distinct roots [MATH: x=0, -1, 1.]

Content:
So, we draw an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shaped graph that passes through these three roots, as follows:

items.title: Graphing a Factored Cubic Curve with Positive Leading Coefficient

sections.normalized_html: Graph the curve corresponding to the equation [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{9}(x-3)(x+2)(x+3).]
sections.readable_text: Graph the curve corresponding to the equation [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{9}(x-3)(x+2)(x+3).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that the function is a product of [MATH: 3] linear binomials, so this function is a cubic function. Moreover, it is a positive cubic because if we were to expand the parentheses, the coefficient of the [MATH: x^3] term would be positive:

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{9}({\color{blue}{x}}-3)({\color{red}{x}}+2)(x+3) = \dfrac 1 9\cdot {\color{blue}{x}}\cdot {\color{red}{x}}\cdot x +\cdots = \dfrac 1 9 x^3+\cdots]

The equation is already in factored form. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that the roots are [MATH: x=3,] [MATH: x=-2,] and [MATH: x=-3.]

We also find the [MATH: y]-intercept of the curve by plugging the value [MATH: x=0] into the equation: [MATH: y|= (1)/(9)(0 − 3)(0 + 2)(0 + 3); = ((− 3)(2)(3))/(9); = − 2]

So, we draw an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shaped graph that passes through the three roots [MATH: x=-3,-2,3] and has the [MATH: y]-intercept [MATH: y=-2,] as follows:

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: x=2] is a root of [MATH: f(x)=x^3-x^2-4x+4,] graph the curve [MATH: y=f(x).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We are told that [MATH: x=2] is a root of [MATH: f(x),] which means that [MATH: (x-2)] is a factor of [MATH: f(x).] So, to find the other roots of [MATH: f(x)] we use synthetic division to divide [MATH: f(x)] by [MATH: (x-2)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: x^{3}|x^{2}|x^{1}|x^{0}; 2|1|− 1|− 4|4; 2|2|− 4; 1|1|− 2|0]

We obtain [MATH: f(x)|= (x − 2)(x^{2} + x − 2); = (x − 2)(x − 1)(x + 2),]

so the other two roots of [MATH: f(x)] are [MATH: x=1] and [MATH: x=-2.]

Now, let's find the [MATH: y]-intercept. To do that, we substitute [MATH: x=0,] and we get [MATH: y|= (0 − 2)(0 − 1)(0 + 2); = (− 2)(− 1)(2); = 4.]

So, we draw an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shaped graph that passes through the three roots [MATH: x=-2,1,2] and has the [MATH: y]-intercept [MATH: y=4,] as follows:

items.title: Graphing an Expanded Cubic Curve with Negative Leading Coefficient

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: x=-1] is a root of [MATH: f(x)=-x^3+4x^2-x-6,] graph the curve [MATH: y=f(x).]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: x=-1] is a root of [MATH: f(x)=-x^3+4x^2-x-6,] graph the curve [MATH: y=f(x).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since [MATH: x=-1] is a root of [MATH: f(x),] this means that [MATH: (x+1)] is a factor of [MATH: f(x),] and therefore, we can begin factoring [MATH: f(x)] by dividing it by [MATH: (x+1).] We use synthetic division, as follows:

[MATH: x^{3}|x^{2}|x^{1}|x^{0}; − 1|− 1|4|− 1|− 6; 1|− 5|6; − 1|5|− 6|0]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The graph of any cubic function [MATH: y = f(x)= ax^3 + bx^2 + cx +d] (where [MATH: a >0]) has a characteristic inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shape, with [MATH: y]-values ranging from [MATH: -\infty] to [MATH: +\infty.] This means that every such function has at least one real root and at most three distinct roots.

Content:
For instance, suppose that we want to plot the graph of [MATH: y = x^3-x.] Then we set [MATH: y=0] to find the roots:
[MATH: x^{3} − x|= 0; x(x^{2} − 1)|= 0; x(x − 1)(x + 1)|= 0]

Content:
By the zero-product rule, we get three distinct roots [MATH: x=0, -1, 1.]

Content:
So, we draw an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shaped graph that passes through these three roots, as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a604e0838d70b66dffb435f418e32ff8]

---

Item 2 — Example: Graphing a Factored Cubic Curve with Positive Leading Coefficient

Example Prompt:
Graph the curve corresponding to the equation [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{9}(x-3)(x+2)(x+3).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice that the function is a product of [MATH: 3] linear binomials, so this function is a cubic function. Moreover, it is a positive cubic because if we were to expand the parentheses, the coefficient of the [MATH: x^3] term would be positive:

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{9}({\color{blue}{x}}-3)({\color{red}{x}}+2)(x+3) = \dfrac 1 9\cdot {\color{blue}{x}}\cdot {\color{red}{x}}\cdot x +\cdots = \dfrac 1 9 x^3+\cdots]

The equation is already in factored form. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that the roots are [MATH: x=3,] [MATH: x=-2,] and [MATH: x=-3.]

We also find the [MATH: y]-intercept of the curve by plugging the value [MATH: x=0] into the equation:
[MATH: y|= (1)/(9)(0 − 3)(0 + 2)(0 + 3); = ((− 3)(2)(3))/(9); = − 2]

So, we draw an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shaped graph that passes through the three roots [MATH: x=-3,-2,3] and has the [MATH: y]-intercept [MATH: y=-2,] as follows:

[IMG: /graphics/b38231503b50fb93cd7da28090bacc11]

Item 5 — Example: Graphing an Expanded Cubic Curve with Positive Leading Coefficient

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: x=2] is a root of [MATH: f(x)=x^3-x^2-4x+4,] graph the curve [MATH: y=f(x).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are told that [MATH: x=2] is a root of [MATH: f(x),] which means that [MATH: (x-2)] is a factor of [MATH: f(x).] So, to find the other roots of [MATH: f(x)] we use synthetic division to divide [MATH: f(x)] by [MATH: (x-2)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: x^{3}|x^{2}|x^{1}|x^{0}; 2|1|− 1|− 4|4; 2|2|− 4; 1|1|− 2|0]

We obtain
[MATH: f(x)|= (x − 2)(x^{2} + x − 2); = (x − 2)(x − 1)(x + 2),]

so the other two roots of [MATH: f(x)] are [MATH: x=1] and [MATH: x=-2.]

Now, let's find the [MATH: y]-intercept. To do that, we substitute [MATH: x=0,] and we get
[MATH: y|= (0 − 2)(0 − 1)(0 + 2); = (− 2)(− 1)(2); = 4.]

So, we draw an inverted [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shaped graph that passes through the three roots [MATH: x=-2,1,2] and has the [MATH: y]-intercept [MATH: y=4,] as follows:

[IMG: /graphics/5a38c33d75c2861769650f404b6307a5]

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}({\color{blue}{x}}+5)(1-{\color{red}{x}})(x+2) = \dfrac 1 2\cdot {\color{blue}{x}}\cdot (-{\color{red}{x}})\cdot x +\cdots = -\dfrac 1 2 x^3+\cdots]

The equation is given in the factored form. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that the roots are [MATH: x=-5,] [MATH: x=1,] and [MATH: x=-2.]

We now find the [MATH: y]-intercept of the curve by plugging the value [MATH: x=0] into the equation:
[MATH: y|= (1)/(2)(0 + 5)(1 − 0)(0 + 2); = ((5)(1)(2))/(2); = 5]

So, we draw an [MATH: {\textsf{S}}]-shaped graph that passes through the three roots [MATH: x=-5,-2,1] and has the [MATH: y]-intercept [MATH: y=5,] as follows:
